- **Date:** 2026-08-27
- **Handoff Version:** 001 (researcher-fall-2026-research_001)
- **Research Scope:** Student baseline, industry use of 3D in visual development, Blender 2025-2026 ecosystem, and pedagogy constraints for a semester-long 3D Integration class at Seneca College (second-year Visual Development).

## Executive Summary

Studios use 3D in visual development as an iteration accelerator, not a production goal: blocking environments, character turnarounds, camera/composition studies, and painted-over renders that feed concept art, previs, and look-dev handoffs. The highest-leverage move for this class is a small set (2-3) of custom Blender tools that remove setup and presentation busywork, so class time goes to design decisions. Pin the class to one Blender LTS (4.5 LTS is the safe pick), teach built-in features for UVs, lighting, cameras, Grease Pencil, and EEVEE iteration, use a short allow-list of add-ons, and structure three escalating projects of 4-5 weeks each.

## 1. Student Baseline

Confirmed (per handoff):
- Second-year Visual Development, Seneca College. Completed a first-semester Digital Tools class.
- Working skills: 3D modeling (edit mode), sculpting, lighting, rendering.
- Primary tool: Blender. Comfort level assumed intermediate-1 (can produce a rendered still from scratch).

Implications for planning:
- Do NOT re-teach modeling, basic materials, or basic lighting. Spend time on *design application* of those skills: composition, scale, silhouette, read-through, and presentation.
- Gaps to probe in week 1 (not assumed known): UV mapping, texture baking, camera language (focal length, depth of field), scene organization/collections, non-destructive workflows (modifiers, node materials), and any 2D-over-3D (paintover) pipeline.
- The differentiating outcome of this class should be: "I can use 3D to explore and communicate design ideas faster, and package the results clearly." That is the portfolio-relevant skill even though portfolio polish is deprioritized this term.

## 2. Industry Landscape

### How studios use 3D in visual development work

- **Role definition:** Visual development artists design the look, tone, atmosphere, characters, environments, and props of a production before it exists; the role spans film, TV, and games (Animation Career Review, updated Nov 2025; Indeed career profile; Concept Art Empire).
- **3D is an expected dimension of the role:** Animation Career Review notes VDAs "typically work in 2D or 3D" with tools including Maya (the 3D work covers environments, characters, and studies) (source: animationcareerreview.com, see Sources).
- **3D blocking / concept-3D as a pipeline stage:** In game production, the standard pipeline is concept art -> 3D blockout -> modeling -> texturing -> engine integration (pixune.com game art pipeline explainer; webenterpreneurs.com pipeline explainer). The blockout stage is where visual-development-level 3D skills plug in: cheap, fast geometry to validate scale, layout, and flow before committed art.
- **Virtuos (contract game studio) explicitly promotes "3D concept art" as a blueprint for cost-effective pre-production** - i.e., 3D studies that de-risk production decisions (virtuosgames.com expert talks, see Sources).
- **Previs:** rough 3D scenes used to plan cameras, blocking, and timing before production - a natural extension skill for VDAs moving into film/TV pipelines (mstudio.ai previs glossary; Blender Studio's own Charge previs blog documents Blender used for film previsualization, studio.blender.org).
- **Look-dev adjacency:** real-time/viewport rendering (EEVEE, engine viewports) is increasingly used to explore material and lighting direction early; studios value artists who can produce a "good enough" render fast and iterate on the design, not the render quality.
- **Paintover workflow:** 3D renders used as underdrawings for 2D paintovers is a widely taught and used bridge between 3D speed and 2D craft. (General industry practice; thin direct sources - flagged as moderate confidence.)

### What studios look for in visual-development hires with 3D capability

Synthesized from role profiles, pipeline write-ups, and BLS guidance (no single public job-post corpus found; confidence: moderate-high on the direction, lower on exact phrasing):

1. **2D craft still comes first.** Drawing, composition, color, and design fundamentals are the gate; 3D is the multiplier. A hire who models well but cannot design is not a VDA hire.
2. **Speed and iteration fluency.** Blocking an environment or character in 3D in minutes, exploring 3-5 directions, and killing weak ones fast. Portfolio of *studies*, not just finished pieces.
3. **Presentation and communication.** Turnarounds (3-view sheets), mood boards, silhouette studies, renders that read at small size. Clean, organized deliverables.
4. **Camera and composition literacy.** Focal length, depth of field, shot types - the 3D viewport is a cheap storyboard tool and studios expect VDAs to use it.
5. **Lighting and color sense in 3D.** Ability to set a believable or stylized light environment quickly (three-point, area/sky, mood lighting) without a lighting artist.
6. **Pipeline awareness.** Naming conventions, collection/scene organization, versioning, exporting assets that others can use. "Opportunities should be best for those who have a wide range of skills" (BLS, quoted in Animation Career Review).
7. **Real-time render fluency.** Comfort with viewport/EEVEE-class rendering as the daily tool, with path-traced (Cycles-class) renders reserved for hero images.

### Market context

- VDA salary range commonly cited at roughly USD 44k-110k depending on studio and region (Animation Career Review citing Glassdoor/SimplyHired; treat as indicative).
- Strongest employment hubs: Los Angeles, New York, and top-10 US metros; Canada (Toronto/Vancouver) is an active animation hub and the local market for Seneca graduates. (ACR; local-market detail from general knowledge - flagged.)

## 3. Blender Ecosystem for Education (2025-2026)

### Version recommendation

- **Pin the class to one LTS release.** Options: **4.5 LTS** (2-year update window, aligned with VFX Reference Platform 2025, widest add-on compatibility) or 5.2 LTS (newest LTS). Recommendation: **4.5 LTS** for Fall 2026 - it is the most proven for classroom add-ons and tutorials, and LTS support extends roughly to 2027. Avoid bleeding-edge releases mid-semester; any version change invalidates student tutorials and add-on behavior. **SUPERSEDED for this program (handoff 021, 2026-08-27): the supported range is now Blender 4.2+ through 5.x (manifest `blender_version_min: 4.2.0`), and the teacher's class build is 5.0 - see the plan and `tools/INSTALL.md`.**
- Blender 4.2+ ships the **Extensions platform**: 600+ free add-ons, drag-and-drop install, offline bundling via `BLENDER_SYSTEM_EXTENSIONS` - this makes a controlled lab add-on set trivial to deploy (blender.org 4.2/4.5 release notes, see Sources).
- Both LTS releases run **EEVEE Next** (real-time GI, displacement, SSS, viewport motion blur) - the workhorse for fast visual-development iteration.

### Built-in features worth teaching (already in core - no add-on needed)

| Feature | Why it matters for a VDA class | Introduced |
|---|---|---|
| EEVEE Next viewport rendering | Real-time GI + fast iteration; the daily "is this design working" tool | 4.2 LTS |
| Grease Pencil (3D sketching) | 3D sketching over blocked scenes; strokes with depth; 4.5 adds Compositor integration, GP nodes in Geometry Nodes, SSAA line quality, animated SVG export | ongoing; big in 4.5 |
| Asset Browser | Class asset library; 4.5 adds one-drag screenshot preview capture - great for building a course asset pack | 3.x; 4.5 |
| UV Editor + Smart UV workflow basics | Students can UV a study mesh and apply a texture; 4.5 shows UV overlays in all modes | core; 4.5 QoL |
| Bake workflows (UV -> texture) | Connects sculpting/high-poly to painted materials; keep to one guided session | core |
| Geometry Nodes (light touch) | Only as "magic": instancing props, scattering, and 4.5's file-import nodes (OBJ/CSV/STL/TXT) for assembling scenes from spreadsheets - teach as an optional accelerator, not a topic | 3.2+; 4.5 |
| Camera controls (focal length, DOF, tracking) | Composition studies in the viewport; cheap storyboard work | core |
| Light tools (4.5: exposure, temperature, normalize) | Faster mood lighting setups | 4.5 |
| Grid Fill + Manifold booleans | Faster cleanup of study geometry | 4.5 |
| Paint color randomization / jitter | Quick stylized surface variation on studies | 4.5 |
| Khronos PBR Neutral tone mapping | Consistent, believable color for presentation renders | 4.2 |

### Add-on allow-list (install via Extensions, pinned versions)

| Add-on | Use | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Smart UV Project (or similar one-click UV) | Kills UV busywork on study meshes | Teach the *concept* once, then let the add-on do it |
| BlenderKit | Free asset library (props, HDRI, materials) for scene assembly | Free tier is sufficient; check license terms for student use |
| A three-point/studio light kit (e.g., any "lights" extension) | Consistent starting lighting in every class file | Alternatively roll our own in the custom starter-scene tool (preferred - fewer third-party deps) |
| Node Tools | Interactive geometry-nodes tweaks (bevel, array, etc.) | Optional; only if GN is touched |
| Decal / matcap utilities | Quick neutral materials for blockouts | Optional |

Guidance: cap the allow-list at 4-5 add-ons. Every additional add-on is a support burden and a version-fragility risk. If a task can be done with a 20-line custom script, prefer the script (see below).

### Custom tools: what to build vs. what to teach

Principle (per teacher intent): custom tools should remove **repetitive setup and presentation busywork**, not replace learning. The tools below are ranked by pedagogy value per development hour.

| Priority | Custom tool | What busywork it removes | Pedagogy value |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Starter Scene** (one click: organized collections, camera + three-point light rig, world/light placeholder, sane render + EEVEE settings, naming conventions applied) | The 20-30 min of per-student, per-assignment scene setup; inconsistent starting points in critique | Very high. Every project starts from an identical, professional-looking scaffold. Also *teaches* scene organization by example. |
| 2 | **Turnaround / 3-view generator** (place N cameras around a selected character/prop, batch-render a labeled grid sheet at chosen resolution) | The single most time-consuming VDA deliverable in the class, done manually today | Very high. Directly produces the industry-standard deliverable; frees students to iterate on the design 3x more. |
| 3 | **Quick Sheet renderer** (render current camera from multiple angles and/or multiple light presets into one contact sheet, with denoise, at low samples) | Manual re-rendering for every design check | High. Encourages "explore 5 directions, keep 2" behavior instead of over-polishing one. |
| 4 | **Grease Pencil sketch pack** (preconfigured stroke styles, line-width/softness presets, one-key line render over the scene) | GP setup friction that discourages 3D sketching | Medium-high. Lowers the barrier to the 3D-sketch habit; pairs well with 4.5 GP improvements. |
| 5 | **Palette extractor** (sample dominant colors from a render into swatches + generate simple material presets) | Manual color-picking for mood boards | Medium. Nice-to-have; supports color-story work. |
| 6 | **File/scene auditor** (check naming, orphan data, collection structure; print a tidy report) | End-of-assignment cleanup | Medium. Instills pipeline habits; cheap to build; also useful for the teacher when collecting work. |

Deliberately NOT custom-built (let built-ins/add-ons cover it): UV unwrap (Smart UV add-on), asset sourcing (BlenderKit), lighting fundamentals (core UI), rendering engine settings (core UI).

Build-order suggestion: Starter Scene (week 1, before any project), Turnaround generator + Quick Sheet (before project 2), sketch pack + palette/auditor (before project 3). Each tool should be a single Python file installable via Extensions, with a 1-page student cheat sheet. Version-pin to the pinned Blender LTS.

## 4. Pedagogy Constraints and Implications

Constraints: 3 h/day, ~16-17 weeks, three project deliverables, do not overwhelm, freedom within guardrails, portfolio polish deprioritized (next semester owns that), custom tools to cut busywork.

Implications:

- **New-skill budget:** introduce at most 1-2 genuinely new skills per project. Everything else is application of known skills.
- **Suggested arc (for the Planner):**
  - Weeks 1-2: foundations and tool tour. Probe UV/camera/composition gaps. Build/demonstrate Starter Scene + Quick Sheet. One guided bake + paintover session. Low-stakes "study sprint" (not a graded project): 2D concept -> 3D block -> render -> paintover, done in one class day.
  - Weeks 3-6, **Project 1 - Environment study:** one designed location, blocked and lit in 3D, 3-5 directional studies via Quick Sheet, 1 hero render + paintover, mood board. Freedom: any subject within a provided guardrail list (e.g., "a place where [story beat] happens").
  - Weeks 7-11, **Project 2 - Character or prop design package:** design development in 3D with Turnaround generator (3-view sheet, expression/variant studies, silhouette check), material exploration, 2 hero renders. Midterm critique ~week 8.
  - Weeks 12-16, **Project 3 - Scene/mood piece:** a short blocked scene (2-4 shots or one long take) using cameras, GP sketching accents, and light mood; deliver as an animatic-style still sequence or short loop. This is the capstone "visual development for a story" deliverable.
  - Week 17: final crit and reflection (process, not polish).
- **Deliverable format (all projects):** organized .blend (auditor-checked), 1 presentation sheet (turnarounds or contact sheet), 1-2 hero renders, 5-minute talk-through. Explicitly *not*: 4K polished finals, full animation, or game-ready assets.
- **Guardrails for freedom:** fixed deliverable types and due dates; free subject matter within a curated prompt list; required process checkpoints (week-1 thumbnail review, week-2 blockout review per project) so students cannot drift.
- **Anti-overwhelm rules:** one LTS version; one add-on allow-list; tools introduced the week before their first use; office-hours "tool clinic" slot; every custom tool ships with a 1-page cheat sheet and a demo file.
- **Assessment tilt (suggested 60/40):** design thinking and iteration evidence (60%) / technical execution and presentation (40%). Rewards the intended behavior: many good studies beat one perfect render.

## 5. Prioritized Recommendations

| Priority | Recommendation | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| High | Pin Blender 4.5 LTS class-wide; deploy via portable install or system extensions bundle | Stability, tutorial compatibility, 2-year support window, easy lab deployment (blender.org 4.5 notes) |
| High | Build Starter Scene + Turnaround generator + Quick Sheet as the three core custom tools | Highest pedagogy value per dev hour; removes the two biggest busywork sinks (setup, presentation) |
| High | Teach Grease Pencil 3D sketching as a first-class skill | 4.5 made GP a real tool (Compositor pass, GP nodes, SSAA); it is the fastest bridge from 2D VDA craft to 3D thinking |
| High | Structure 3 projects of 4-5 weeks with fixed deliverable types, free subject matter, and 2 process checkpoints per project | Matches constraints; keeps freedom within guardrails; prevents overwhelm |
| Medium | Keep add-ons to a 4-5 item allow-list (Smart UV, BlenderKit, light kit, Node Tools) | Support burden and version fragility scale with add-on count |
| Medium | One guided bake + paintover session in weeks 1-2 | Closes the 2D/3D bridge early; paintover is an industry-standard VDA skill (moderate-source confidence) |
| Medium | Add file/scene auditor and palette extractor as project-3 tools | Instills pipeline habits; cheap to build; useful for teacher grading |
| Low | Geometry Nodes as optional accelerator only (instancing, 4.5 file-import nodes) | High ceiling, high cognitive cost; wrong default for a design-focused class |
| Low | Brief Cycles comparison session (one hero-render difference demo) | Students should know when to switch engines without learning both deeply |

## 6. Open Questions / Uncertainties

- No public corpus of studio VDA job posts was directly crawled; the "what studios look for" list is a synthesis of role profiles and pipeline write-ups (moderate confidence). If stronger evidence is needed, scrape 20-30 live postings (ArtStation Jobs, CGSociety, LinkedIn) for Toronto/LA/remote VDA roles.
- Seneca's exact Digital Tools first-semester syllabus was not available; the assumed baseline (modeling/sculpt/light/render) comes from the handoff only. Confirm UV, camera, and organization coverage with the Digital Tools instructor.
- Lab hardware/GPU specs unknown; EEVEE Next performance and class render budgets depend on this.
- Whether the program prefers Maya literacy (industry-standard in film) was not in scope; this plan assumes Blender as the single 3D tool, per the handoff. Worth a one-line confirmation with the program advisor.
- 5.x Blender releases exist (5.0-5.2 LTS) as of mid-2026; add-on compatibility and tutorial coverage for 5.x in the education niche were not verified. 4.5 LTS remains the recommended pin unless the instructor wants the newest LTS.

## Sources

- blender.org/download/releases/4-5/ : Blender 4.5 LTS release notes (Vulkan, Grease Pencil upgrades, UV overlays, asset browser capture, Geometry Nodes import nodes, extensions platform, VFX Platform 2025 alignment)
- blender.org/download/releases/4-2/ : Blender 4.2 LTS release notes (EEVEE Next, Extensions platform, Khronos PBR Neutral, VFX Platform 2024 alignment)
- animationcareerreview.com/articles/visual-development-artist-career-profile : VDA role definition, 2D/3D scope, BLS job-outlook guidance, salary context (updated Nov 2025)
- indeed.com/career-advice/finding-a-job/what-is-visual-development-artist : VDA role summary (page blocked direct fetch; summary verified via search result snippet)
- conceptartempire.com/what-is-vis-dev-artist/ : VDA vs concept artist distinction in animation (via search snippet)
- virtuosgames.com/news/expert-talks-expert-talks-3d-concept-art/ : studio-side case for 3D concept art in game pre-production (via search result)
- pixune.com/blog/game-art-pipeline/ and webenterpreneurs.com/from-concept-to-engine-the-game-art-pipeline-explained/ : standard game art pipeline stages (concept -> blockout -> model -> texture -> engine)
- mstudio.ai/glossary/previs : previs definition (rough 3D for camera/blocking/timing planning)
- studio.blender.org/blog/charge-previsualization/ : Blender used for film previsualization (Blender Studio)
- extensions.blender.org : Blender extensions platform (600+ free add-ons, offline bundling)

Note: items marked "via search snippet" or "general industry practice" are lower-confidence than directly fetched pages.

- [x] Covers popular (industry-standard) and niche (Blender-ecosystem) angles

## Part B - Production / Studio Terminology Mapping

Purpose: rename plan deliverables to real studio production language (Toronto + general industry). Confidence levels are honest; where web verification was thin (search engines stripped quoted niche terms), confidence is marked moderate and the term is flagged for the teacher's spot-check against live Toronto VDA postings (a verification step already in class-structure.md).

### Mapping table

| Plan term (current) | Recommended production term | One-line definition | Character / prop | Standard? | Confidence |
|---------------------|---------------------------|--------------------|------------------|-----------|------------|
| presentation sheet (P2) | **turnaround** (or "character turnaround" / "3-view turnaround") | Character/prop shown front, side, back (often 3/4) on one sheet so form reads in solid color. | Both (character primary) | Industry-standard, universal across 2D/3D/games. | High |
| presentation sheet (P2, full ref) | **model sheet** (2D traditional) / **character sheet** (3D) | The complete character reference: turnaround + proportions + expression set + color callout. | Character | Industry-standard; "model sheet" is the classic 2D-animation term, "character sheet" common in 3D. | High |
| (teacher's vocabulary) **fun sheet / fun pack** | **fun sheet** (two words) | North American animation usage for a character presentation sheet, i.e. a turnaround/model sheet delivered as a flat sheet. | Character | **"Fun sheet" (two words) is real regional/North American animation usage; "funpack" (one word) was flagged NON-STANDARD here - SUPERSEDED for this program (handoff 012): the teacher's studio uses "funpack", which is now the primary deliverable name (see the verdict note below).** | Moderate (regional usage; thin public web corpus) |
| contact sheet (P1 studies, P3 shots) | **contact sheet** (keep) | A single sheet composing many frames/studies in a grid, each labeled; in film it is a strip of stills, in VDA a grid of directional studies. | Both | Industry-standard (film + animation + games). Keep as-is. | High |
| mood board (P1) | **mood board** (keep) or **art direction board** | References + palette establishing visual direction before production. "Art direction board" is the more production-side name; in 3D the nearest pipeline phase is **look development (lookdev)** references. | Both | "Mood board" is universally understood; "art direction board" is production-standard in TV/film. | High (mood board) / Moderate (art direction board) |
| prop deliverable (P2 prop track) | **prop sheet** / **prop turnaround** | Prop shown in 2-4 angles with scale reference and material callout, for consistency across shots. | Prop | Used in production, less canonized than character terms; "prop turnaround" is the safest standard form. | Moderate |

| blocked scene (P3) | **previs blockout** (a.k.a. **previs**) | Roughly blocked scene with rough camera moves to verify composition, scale, and story beats before final work. | Scene/shot | Industry-standard in VFX/film ("previs" is a universal noun). High. |
| blocked scene (P3, VDA-flavored) | **camera study** / **camera block** | A composed camera setup of a blocked scene, evaluated for framing, focal length, and depth - the VDA-specific reading of a blockout. | Scene/shot | Standard in visual development studios. | High |
| shot-sequence contact sheet (P3) | **shot sequence** (on a contact sheet) | Shots presented in story order, each labeled with type and purpose; standard film/TV delivery language. | Scene/shot | Industry-standard. | High |
| hero render (all projects) | **beauty render** (a.k.a. beauty pass) or keep "hero render" | The final-quality still render of the shot/subject; "beauty" is the 3D pipeline term, "hero" is common in games/marketing. | Both | Both understood; "beauty render" is the 3D production standard. | High |
| paintover (P1/P3) | **paintover** (keep) | A 2D painted pass over a 3D render adding design information (value, mood, correction). | Both | Industry-standard in VDA/VFX; keep. | High |
| style frame (if adopted) | **style frame** | A fully rendered reference frame locking look (light, color, texture, grade) for a shot or sequence. | Scene/shot | Industry-standard in film/TV animation. | High |
| style board (if adopted) | **style board** | A set of style frames establishing the overall look across sequences; used in some game/film pipelines. | Scene/shot | Used, less universal than style frame. | Moderate |

### "Funpack" verdict (explicit, per handoff)

- **"Funpack" as one word is not an industry-standard term.** Do not put it in deliverable names, rubrics, or student-facing docs.
- The legitimate related usage is **"fun sheet"** (two words), a North American (strong Toronto/Canadian and US studio) term for a character presentation/turnaround sheet. It will be understood in Toronto studios, but an international reviewer may not know it.
- **Safe default: use "turnaround" (or "character turnaround" / "model sheet")** in the plan. Mention "fun sheet" in class as the studio shorthand so students hear both, but keep the graded deliverable name standard.
- **SUPERSEDED (handoff 012, 2026-08-27): the teacher - the program's ground truth - has decided that "funpack" (one word) is the primary deliverable name in this course.** The do-not-use guidance above no longer applies to this program's plan files or rubrics; "turnaround" and "fun sheet" (two words) remain accepted aliases. Students are told that sheet terminology varies by studio and to match their target studio's vocabulary when presenting elsewhere.

### Recommended renames (2-3, for the rename pass)

1. **P2 "turnaround/3-view sheet" -> "turnaround"** (character track) and **"prop turnaround"** (prop track). Optionally add "model sheet" as the fuller-reference variant. Avoid "funpack"; teach "fun sheet" as studio slang only. **Superseded by handoff 012: the plan now uses "funpack" as the primary name (character funpack / prop funpack), with "turnaround" and "fun sheet" (two words) as accepted aliases.**
2. **P3 "blocked scene" -> "previs blockout"**, with the sheet called a **"shot sequence (contact sheet)"**. This is the single most industry-accurate rename available and directly matches how VDA work is scoped in studios.
3. **Keep "contact sheet" and "mood board"** (both are already understood industry terms); if a more production-flavored name is wanted for the mood board, use **"art direction board"**.

body:
- **Date:** 2026-08-28
- **Handoff:** 039 (Researcher, modern-teaching-techniques)
- **Purpose:** Synthesize evidence-based teaching techniques into concrete, writable rules for an AI subagent that produces educational content for this course's students.
- **Scope note:** The task brief says "3D web integration projects". This project is 3D Integration (Blender, Visual Development, Seneca Fall 2026). The techniques below apply to both; where a pattern is web-specific, it is flagged.
- **Constraint honored:** every recommendation is translated into a *writing rule* a text-based AI tutor can execute, not a classroom ritual.

## Executive Summary

The strongest-evidence techniques in 2024-2026 all reduce to one design stance for a text-based AI tutor: **make the student do the thinking, in small well-sequenced doses, in a voice that makes them feel safe and curious.** Retrieval practice, distributed and interleaved sequencing, low-extraneous-load presentation, autonomy-supportive language, humor as connective tissue, Socratic questioning, and metacognitive prompts are the highest-leverage levers - and every one is expressible as a rule an LLM can follow when writing a lesson.

## 1. Cognitive Science (the protocol's spine)

### 1.1 Retrieval practice (testing effect)
- **Why it works:** Actively pulling information out of memory strengthens it more than re-reading it, and it calibrates the learner's own judgment of what they know.
- **Evidence:** Roediger & Karpicke (2006) - retrieval beat restudying even when students believed restudying was better. Dunlosky et al. (2013) review of ten learning techniques ranked retrieval practice and distributed practice as the two highest-yield general techniques.
- **AI-tutor rules:**
  - Never end a concept block without 1-3 retrieval questions ("without looking back, what happens if...").
  - Use question-first structure: pose, then reveal.
  - Use delayed retrieval: revisit a 1-4-weeks-old concept inside this week's content.
  - Prefer "do this step, then here's why" over "here's why, now do this."

### 1.2 Spaced repetition (distributed practice)
- **Why it works:** Spreading exposure across days/weeks builds durable memory; massed review decays fast.
- **Evidence:** Cepeda et al. (2006) meta-analysis - spaced beat massed practice in 259 of 271 comparisons.
- **AI-tutor rules:**
  - Every lesson file carries a "revisit" hook: 1-2 lines referencing a concept from 1-4 weeks earlier.
  - Rotate a small review set across the 13 weeks rather than front-loading.
  - Because a text AI cannot schedule sessions, spacing is achieved *by design*: each unit must re-use prior concepts in a new context (spacing by reuse).

### 1.3 Interleaving
- **Why it works:** Mixing related problem types forces discrimination of "which approach fits", not just execution of one routine.
- **Evidence:** Rohrer & Taylor (2007) - shuffling math problems improved learning and transfer versus blocking by type.
- **AI-tutor rules:**
  - In exercise lists, alternate A / B / A rather than all-A-then-all-B.
  - When presenting a task menu, explicitly vary the design problems across slots.
  - Flag interleaving in the plan: a task that mixes camera + scale + composition beats a camera-only task.

### 1.4 Dual coding (Paivio)
- **Why it works:** Verbal + visual/imaginal channels encode the same idea twice, giving two retrieval routes.
- **Evidence:** Paivio (1971, 1986); extended by Mayer's multimedia / modality-effect work.
- **AI-tutor rules (text-only):**
  - Convert every spatial/3D concept into a strong verbal image plus a simple ASCII/word diagram where useful.
  - Ask the student to sketch (2D concepting is already a course habit): "sketch the light direction before you move it."
  - Prefer concrete visual anchors over abstract terms: "the light is like a lamp on a stand aimed at your subject."

### 1.5 Cognitive load theory (Sweller)
- **Why it works:** Working memory is small; extraneous load steals capacity from learning (germane load).
- **Evidence:** Sweller (1988); worked-example and split-attention effects (Chandler & Sweller 1992); the expertise-reversal effect (Kalyuga et al. 2003) means novices and experts need different support.
- **AI-tutor rules:**
  - One learning goal per content block (matches the course anti-overwhelm rule).
  - Worked example first for new concepts: full example, then a "fill the missing step" version, then solo (fading).
  - Strip extraneous load: no filler, no unexplained jargon, one idea per sentence.
  - Scale support to level: these are second-year students (not novices) - give more challenge where they are competent, more scaffolding where they are not (expertise reversal in reverse).

### 1.6 Desirable difficulties (Bjork)
- **Why it works:** Effortful-but-productive retrieval and interleaving feel harder but yield better long-term retention.
- **Evidence:** Bjork & Bjork (2011).
- **AI-tutor rules:**
  - Do not smooth out every stumble. Let the student struggle for a defined window before the answer.
  - Provide a hint ladder (vague -> specific -> near-answer) instead of instant answers.

## 2. Motivation

### 2.1 Growth mindset (Dweck)
- **Why it works:** Framing ability as improvable shifts students from "proving myself" to "improving."
- **Evidence:** Dweck (2006); but Sisk et al. (2018) meta-analysis found small effects (~d=0.08), and Yeager et al. (2023, "Growth mindset 3.0") reframed it as a "not-yet" mindset tied to effort strategies rather than slogans.
- **AI-tutor rules:**
  - Praise process and strategy, never talent: "that's a smart decomposition", not "you're so talented."
  - Use "not yet" language on failure: "the render looks flat because the key light is doing the fill's job - not yet, try this."
  - Never say "easy" or "obvious" or "anyone can do this."

### 2.2 Self-determination theory (Deci & Ryan)
- **Why it works:** Intrinsic motivation requires satisfying autonomy, competence, and relatedness.
- **Evidence:** Deci & Ryan (2000); Deci, Koestner & Ryan (1999) meta-analysis - extrinsic rewards can undermine intrinsic motivation (overjustification effect).
- **AI-tutor rules:**
  - Autonomy: offer a choice within guardrails ("pick one of these three and justify it") - matches the course freedom-within-guardrails rule.
  - Competence: sequence so the student succeeds often; small wins.
  - Relatedness: the voice must feel like a person, not a manual.
  - Avoid reward language (points/badges); let the work be the reward.

### 2.3 Psychological safety (Edmondson)
- **Why it works:** Students who fear judgment stop asking questions and stop taking creative risks.
- **Evidence:** Edmondson (2019); Edmondson & Lei (2017, HBR) on learning behaviors.
- **AI-tutor rules:**
  - Normalize mistakes: "this is a common first attempt" / "everyone's first blockout looks like a box on a stick."
  - Critique the work, praise the thinking; never the person.
  - End each block with a low-stakes question that signals "no question is dumb."
  - For a text AI, safety = never mocking, never condescending, always a recovery path.

### 2.4 Intrinsic motivation + feedback (Hattie & Timperley)
- **Why it works:** Feedback that answers "where am I going / how am I going / where to next" drives learning more than grades or praise.
- **Evidence:** Hattie & Timperley (2007) review of 700+ studies.
- **AI-tutor rules:**
  - Structure every feedback moment as: task goal, current state, next action.
  - Be specific: "the prop reads small because it's the same scale as the character", not "make the prop bigger."
  - Close the loop: reference earlier feedback and ask "did moving the light change the mood?"

## 3. Humor and Engagement

### 3.1 Humor in learning
- **Why it works:** Light humor lowers the affective filter, builds rapport, and makes a concept memorable as a story.
- **Evidence:** Martin's humor-styles research (Martin 2007) separates affiliative (warm, shared) from aggressive (punchline-at-someone's-expense) humor. Classroom research is mixed - humor aids engagement and perceived learning, but effects on test scores are small or inconsistent.
- **AI-tutor rules:**
  - Use affiliative, self-deprecating, observational humor. Never aggressive or "dumb-student" jokes.
  - Humor is seasoning, not the meal: 1-2 jokes per block, always tied to the concept.
  - Comedic timing = set a small expectation, then a gentle twist that is the lesson ("you'll be tempted to just crank the light... and that's exactly what makes the scene flat").
  - Never make fun of the student's work, level, or choices.

### 3.2 Storytelling (narrative)
- **Why it works:** Narrative transport engages attention and gives structure; stories make the abstract concrete.
- **Evidence:** Bruner (1986) on narrative as a mode of thought; Green & Brock (2000) narrative-transport literature - stories reduce counter-arguing.
- **AI-tutor rules:**
  - Open each lesson with a 2-3 sentence scenario ("it's 10pm, the art director just sent back a note...").
  - Frame design decisions as a story arc: setup (brief) -> complication (constraint) -> resolution (your solution).
  - Use the student's project as the story: "your environment is a character - what's its motivation?"

### 3.3 Analogies
- **Why it works:** Analogies map a known structure onto an unknown one, giving a working model before the formal definition.
- **Evidence:** Gick & Holyoak (1980) analogy-cue effect; Gentner's structure-mapping theory.
- **AI-tutor rules:**
  - Lead with the analogy, then the formal term: "the camera is a window you can move (then: a virtual camera with focal length, position, rotation)."
  - Source analogies from the student's world: cooking, driving, photography, music.
  - Flag the analogy's limit: "the analogy breaks down here - in Blender, X is different."
  - Never let an analogy replace precision; always land on the real term.

## 4. Socratic Method + Active Learning

### 4.1 Socratic questioning
- **Why it works:** Questions lead the learner to discover the rule rather than receive it, producing deeper and more transferable understanding.
- **Evidence:** Long-standing method; Socratic-questioning research in CS education shows gains in conceptual understanding.
- **AI-tutor rules:**
  - Ask one question at a time; do not stack.
  - Rotate types: "what would happen if..." / "how do you know?" / "what's another way?" / "why does that work?"
  - Use the question to expose a misconception, not to quiz.
  - If the student is stuck, ask a smaller question, not a hint (Socratic, not rescue).

### 4.2 Guided discovery / scaffolding
- **Why it works:** Support is strongest where the learner is weakest and is removed as competence grows (fading), so the learner internalizes the strategy.
- **Evidence:** Wood, Bruner & Ross (1976) on tutoring and the zone of proximal development.
- **AI-tutor rules:**
  - Model once, then a guided "do it with me", then "do it alone" (the fade sequence).
  - Keep the scaffold visible and removable; do not bury the answer in the explanation.

### 4.3 Productive failure (Kapur)
- **Why it works:** Struggling with a complex problem before instruction builds richer schemas and better transfer.
- **Evidence:** Kapur (2008); strongest effects in complex problem-solving contexts, mixed for simple skill acquisition - so use it on design problems, not on button-clicking.
- **AI-tutor rules:**
  - For design decisions, let the student attempt and fail before showing the canonical approach.
  - Cap the struggle: after 1-2 failed attempts, give the structured hint ladder.

### 4.4 Peer instruction (Mazur)
- **Why it works:** Explaining an answer to a peer is a retrieval act; disagreeing forces re-evaluation.
- **Evidence:** Mazur (1997); peer instruction widely adopted across STEM.
- **AI-tutor rules (solo, text):**
  - Simulate the peer move: after the student answers, ask "now argue the opposite case for 2 sentences" - a self-peer-explanation.
  - Present two plausible answers and have the student pick and defend (think-choose-explain).

## 5. Metacognition and Reflection

### 5.1 Metacognition (Flavell)
- **Why it works:** Thinking about one's own thinking improves strategy selection and self-regulation.
- **Evidence:** Flavell (1979); metacognitive-prompting research shows gains in STEM problem-solving.
- **AI-tutor rules:**
  - Add a short "think about your thinking" prompt after key steps ("why did that work? what would you do differently next time?").
  - Ask the student to predict before acting ("before you render, what do you expect to see?"), then compare.

### 5.2 Learning journals / reflection
- **Why it works:** Externalizing the process consolidates it and creates a record for the learner and teacher.
- **Evidence:** Schon (1983) reflective practitioner; reflection journals standard in professional and design education.
- **AI-tutor rules:**
  - End each lesson with a 3-line reflection prompt (what I did / what I learned / what I'd try next).
  - Keep it short and specific to the week's task, not generic.

### 5.3 Self-assessment (Boud)
- **Why it works:** Judging one's own work against criteria builds internal standards and reduces dependence on the teacher.
- **Evidence:** Boud (2001) on enhancing the power of self-assessment.
- **AI-tutor rules:**
  - Give the student the rubric criteria and ask them to self-score before the AI gives its view.
  - Ask "which criterion is your weakest, and what's your evidence?"

## 6. Modern Pedagogical Frameworks

### 6.1 Universal Design for Learning (UDL)
- **Why it works:** Offering multiple means of engagement, representation, and action/expression accommodates individual differences by design.
- **Evidence:** CAST UDL Guidelines (2018) - three principles: engagement, representation, action/expression.
- **AI-tutor rules:**
  - Offer multiple entry points to the same goal (a visual path and a step path).
  - Vary representation: text, diagram, analogy, example.
  - Vary expression: let the student show understanding by doing, writing, or sketching.

### 6.2 Project-based learning (PBL)
- **Why it works:** Learning by solving a real, extended, complex problem builds deeper knowledge and transfer.
- **Evidence:** Thomas (2000) review of project-based learning research; PBL World (pblworld.org).
- **AI-tutor rules:**
  - Anchor every concept to the student's actual project, not an abstract example.
  - Keep the driving question visible at the top of each lesson.

### 6.3 Flipped classroom
- **Why it works:** Moving low-order content (reading/watching) to self-paced time frees class time for high-order doing.
- **Evidence:** Flipped Learning Network (flippedlearning.org); flipped-classroom research on engagement.
- **AI-tutor rules:**
  - Front-load the "what" (self-paced reading block) and reserve the "do" for the interactive portion.
  - Treat the lesson doc as the pre-work; the AI's live role is the doing and feedback.

### 6.4 Mastery learning
- **Why it works:** Advancing only when the current concept is solid prevents error accumulation.
- **Evidence:** Bloom (1968) "learning for mastery" (2 sigma study).
- **AI-tutor rules:**
  - Gate the next block on a minimal "show me you can..." check, not on time.
  - If the check fails, loop back with the hint ladder, not a re-lecture.

## 7. What the Best Coding Instructors Do

| Instructor | Structure signature | Takeaway for the AI tutor |
|---|---|---|
| freeCodeCamp (freecodecamp.org) | Curriculum as sequenced, project-gated modules; learn by building; zero-pollution environment | Gate progression on a working artifact, not a quiz; keep the "build" front and center |
| The Odin Project (theodinproject.com) | Path-based curriculum, project-first, emphasizes self-direction and reading docs | Teach the student to navigate real docs; project-first, concept-second |
| Codecademy (codecademy.com) | Interactive in-browser IDE, immediate feedback loop, concept drills | Instant feedback after each micro-step; keep the loop tight (do -> see result -> adjust) |
| MIT OCW 6.0001 (ocw.mit.edu) | Lecture + recitation + problem sets; office-hours culture; weekly labs | Pair every concept with a problem set of increasing difficulty; make help-seeking normal |
| CS50 (Harvard) | High-production lectures, live coding, emphasis on "why" over "how", office hours | Explain the *why* of each tool; production quality in content; model struggle live |
| Blender Guru / default cube (3D) | 12-hour project-first tutorial: one continuous project, concepts introduced only when needed | Introduce tools only at the moment they are needed in the student's project - just-in-time, not just-in-case |

**Cross-instructor patterns to adopt:**
1. Project-first: concepts are introduced only when the student needs them for their build (just-in-time).
2. Tight feedback loop: do a micro-step, see the result immediately, adjust.
3. Progression gated on artifacts, not time or quizzes.
4. Normalized help-seeking: office hours / docs are part of the curriculum, not a failure state.
5. Production-quality content: the craft of the presentation signals the craft of the discipline.

## 8. Voice and Persona (Tim Urban, Derek Muller, 3Blue1Brown, Simon Sinek)

| Creator | Voice technique | AI-tutor rule |
|---|---|---|
| Tim Urban (Wait But Why) | Long-form curiosity-driven narration; "wait, but why?" reframes the abstract as a story; self-aware, slightly rambly energy | Open with a question the student already half-asks; let the answer unfold in layers rather than a flat list |
| Derek Muller (Veritasium) | Counter-intuitive hook first; shows a surprising result, then explains it; high production, direct-to-camera intimacy | Lead with the surprising outcome of a 3D operation, then explain the mechanism |
| 3Blue1Brown (Grant Sanderson) | Visual intuition before notation; builds concepts by animation; extremely slow, deliberate pacing; "you can't unsee it" moments | Build intuition before jargon; one idea at a time; let the student "see" the math/space before naming it |
| Simon Sinek | Starts with WHY before how/what; meaning-driven framing; conviction and simplicity | Open each lesson with the why (design outcome) before the how (Blender steps) |

**Voice spec for the subagent:**
- Tone: a sharp, slightly wry friend who is genuinely excited about 3D. Confident but never condescending.
- Rhythm: short sentences for action steps; longer, flowing sentences for "why" explanations.
- Open with the outcome or the question, not the tool name.
- Use "you" as the default; "we" when modeling a step together.
- One joke or light aside per block, max. Always in service of the concept.
- Never: corporate filler ("leveraging", "utilize"), exclamation-heavy hype, or fake familiarity ("like, so basically").

## 9. Cross-Cutting Pitfalls (from the research)
- **Over-praise:** Dweck's own later work and Sisk et al. (2018) warn that generic praise and growth-mindset slogans can backfire. Praise specifics, not the person.
- **Humor with mixed evidence:** humor lifts engagement, not reliably test scores. Use it as connective tissue, not the payload.
- **Productive failure is context-sensitive:** strong for complex design problems, weak for rote skill. Do not let students flail on button-clicking.
- **AI deskilling:** if the AI always answers, the student stops generating. Protect productive struggle with the hint ladder.
- **Expertise reversal:** beginners and experts need different support. These are second-year students - calibrate up.
- **Illusion of knowledge:** easy lookup (copy-paste, AI answers) feels like knowing. Retrieval practice is the antidote.
- **Split-attention and extraneous load:** clutter, unexplained jargon, and multi-goal blocks silently destroy learning (Sweller).

## 10. Protocol Recommendations for the AI Tutor Subagent

### 10.1 Persona
A sharp, slightly wry friend who loves 3D. Confident, warm, never condescending. Speaks to "you". One light aside per block. Opens with the why or the question, not the tool.

### 10.2 Lesson structure (per unit)
1. **Hook** - a surprising outcome or a question the student already half-asks (2-3 sentences).
2. **Why** - the design reason, in plain language (Sinek's why-first).
3. **Concept** - one idea, intuition before jargon, an analogy + its limit, a verbal/ASCII image (dual coding).
4. **Do** - a micro-step with immediate feedback, project-anchored (just-in-time).
5. **Check** - 1-3 retrieval questions + a self-assessment against one rubric criterion (mastery gate).
6. **Reflect** - 3-line reflection prompt (what I did / learned / would try next).
7. **Revisit** - 1-2 lines connecting to a 1-4-weeks-old concept (spacing).

### 10.3 Voice rules
- Short sentences for steps, longer for explanations.
- Praise process, never talent. Use "not yet" on failure.
- Never: "easy", "obvious", "anyone can do this", corporate filler, exclamation hype.
- Critique the work, praise the thinking.

### 10.4 Question rules
- One question at a time; rotate question types.
- If stuck, ask a smaller question, then offer the hint ladder (vague -> specific -> near-answer).
- After an answer, ask the student to defend it or argue the opposite (self-peer-explanation).

### 10.5 Load and safety rules
- One learning goal per block.
- Strip extraneous load: no filler, one idea per sentence, define every term on first use.
- Normalize mistakes; always give a recovery path; never mock.

### 10.6 Evidence-to-rule mapping (quick reference)
| Evidence | Rule |
|---|---|
| Retrieval practice (Roediger & Karpicke) | End every block with retrieval questions |
| Spacing (Cepeda) | Revisit hooks to 1-4-weeks-old concepts |
| Interleaving (Rohrer) | Alternate problem types in exercise lists |
| Dual coding (Paivio) | Verbal image + diagram + analogy for every spatial concept |
| Cognitive load (Sweller) | One goal per block; worked example then fade |
| Desirable difficulties (Bjork) | Hint ladder, not instant answers |
| SDT (Deci & Ryan) | Choice within guardrails; no reward language |
| Psychological safety (Edmondson) | Normalize mistakes; critique work not person |
| Feedback (Hattie & Timperley) | Goal / current state / next action |
| Socratic + scaffolding (Wood, Bruner & Ross) | One question at a time; model then fade |
| Metacognition (Flavell, Boud) | Predict-then-act prompts; self-scoring |
| UDL (CAST) | Multiple means of representation and expression |

## 11. Sources

body:
- **Date:** 2026-08-28
- **Handoff Version:** 027
- **Research Scope:** a candidate bank of historically iconic, cross-cultural events fertile for fantastical/futuristic/mythological reinterpretation, with a week-mapping suggestion and a constraints summary for the Planner/Executor.

## Executive Summary
A 30-candidate bank of encyclopedia-grade events spanning East Asian, Central Asian, African, South Asian, Middle Eastern, Indigenous Americas, and European traditions, each with a strong gender and/or social-class angle and at least one fantastical or mythological hook. A suggested week-to-candidate sketch aligns environment-leaning prompts to P1 (W3-W5), character/prop-leaning prompts to P2 (W6-W8), and story-moment prompts to P3 (W9-W12). Constraints (3-hour/no-homework, tool availability, funpack terminology, 60/40 tilt) are summarized for the lesson docs. Prompts remain placeholders until the teacher finalizes them.

## How to Use This Bank
- Each candidate lists: **Name**, **Era**, **Culture/Region**, **Why it works as a 3D subject** (1-2 sentences), **Gender/class angle**, **Fantastical hook(s)** (futuristic and/or mythological), and a **Content note** flag where needed.
- Candidates are grouped by region for scanning, not ranked. The **Top 5** (section 8) are the strongest all-rounders.
- A candidate can serve more than one project; the mapping in section 9 is a starting sketch, not a fixed assignment.
- Keep prompts as **story-anchored beats** ("a place where [event] happens", "a character central to [event]", "the moment of [event]"), per the plan's freedom guardrails. The event supplies the story anchor; the student supplies the design.
- Every prompt is a placeholder: the teacher finalizes wording. This bank is raw material for the Planner, not student-facing copy.

## 1. East Asia

**1. Meiji Restoration (1868)** -- Japan
- **Why it works:** a castle town becoming a modern capital in one generation; strong before/after spatial contrast and a clear story beat.
- **Gender/class:** the fall of the samurai aristocracy, the rise of merchants and commoners; women's education and public roles expanding.
- **Hooks:** futuristic neo-Tokyo where the old elite ride the new trains; the sun (Amaterasu) returning as a machine.
- **Content note:** none.

**2. Battle of Sekigahara (1600)** -- Japan
- **Why it works:** a vast open field framed by mountains, ideal for scale, flow, and silhouette studies.
- **Gender/class:** daimyo and rōnin vs. conscripted commoner ashigaru infantry; the class of the foot soldier.
- **Hooks:** a celestial battlefield; a mecha castle on the ridge.
- **Content note:** none (combat as backdrop, not the selling point).

**3. Imjin War / Battle of Hansan Island (1592)** -- Korea
- **Why it works:** a coastal naval clash with fast, maneuverable warships; strong horizon, water, and ship-silhouette design.
- **Gender/class:** commoner militias and warrior-monks vs. an aristocratic court; the admiral who rose from a provincial command (class mobility through skill).
- **Hooks:** the armored "turtle ship" reimagined as a living creature or a submersible; the sea-god Hanul.
- **Content note:** none (navy vs. navy; keep violence abstract).

**4. Japanese castle town / Himeji (Edo period)** -- Japan
- **Why it works:** a white heron castle over a planned town; a rich, layered environment for scale and flow.
- **Gender/class:** castle lords vs. town merchants; women of the inner castle (oka) vs. the public town.
- **Hooks:** a floating castle; the castle as a living god with a spirit in the keep.
- **Content note:** none.

**5. Fall of the Ming / Fall of Beijing (1644)** -- China
- **Why it works:** the Forbidden City as a monumental environment; a dramatic political turning point.
- **Gender/class:** peasant rebels (Li Zicheng's army) vs. the imperial court; the fate of court ladies.
- **Hooks:** a futuristic Peking; the dragon-emperor as a machine.
- **Content note:** YES -- sack of the city and the fate of the imperial family; frame as political transition, avoid graphic violence.

**6. Fall of the Song / Battle of Yamen (1279)** -- China
- **Why it works:** a huge naval engagement on open water; strong for camera and composition studies.
- **Gender/class:** Empress Li, the last Song empress-regent (a female sovereign in a male line); the sailor class on the sea.
- **Hooks:** a fleet of floating cities; a dragon-boat armada as mythological warships.
- **Content note:** YES -- the drowning of the empress and her son; handle the historical death with care, keep the fantastical hook forward.

**7. 1964 Tokyo Olympics** -- Japan
- **Why it works:** a postwar reconstruction moment; a stadium and city in motion, full of energy.
- **Gender/class:** female athletes and workers in a rebuilding economy; a national project of common effort.
- **Hooks:** retro-futurist Tokyo; a torii gate arching over the stadium.
- **Content note:** none.

## 2. Central Asia

**8. Mongol conquest / Silk Road trade (13th c.)** -- Khwarazmian Empire
- **Why it works:** a vast steppe meeting a caravan city; strong for scale and horizon studies.
- **Gender/class:** nomadic vs. settled class structures; the trader vs. the warrior; women of the encampment.
- **Hooks:** a steppe of sky-cities; horse-spirits as mythological mounts.
- **Content note:** YES -- conquest and destruction of cities; frame as trade and movement, not slaughter.

**9. Samarkand, Timurid era (15th c.)** -- Central Asia
- **Why it works:** turquoise domes and a bustling bazaar; a colorful, high-contrast environment.
- **Gender/class:** merchants and artisans vs. the court; the market as a mixed-class space; women of the souk.
- **Hooks:** a futuristic oasis of blue tilework; a divine king's court of scholars.
- **Content note:** none.

## 3. Africa

**10. Battle of Adwa (1896)** -- Ethiopia
- **Why it works:** mountain passes and highland fortifications; a decisive defensive victory with strong topography.
- **Gender/class:** Empress Taitu Betul, a documented female military leader; Ras Alula, a general of peasant origin (class mobility through merit).
- **Hooks:** a futuristic highland fortress; the Lion of Judah as a mythological guardian.
- **Content note:** none (a celebrated Ethiopian victory; keep combat abstract).

**11. Great Zimbabwe (11th-15th c.)** -- Shona, Zimbabwe
- **Why it works:** dry-stone walls and a great enclosure; an iconic, self-contained environment with strong mass and flow.
- **Gender/class:** gold/ivory trade networks; women as potters and traders.
- **Hooks:** a city in the sky (the ruin's name links to "birds"); a futuristic renaissance of the stone city.
- **Content note:** none.

**12. Battle of Tondibi (1591)** -- Songhai Empire, Mali/Niger
- **Why it works:** a river and steppe battlefield; strong for a "crossing" story beat.
- **Gender/class:** the legacy of enslaved soldiers (black Mamluk descendants) in the Moroccan army vs. the Songhai court; women of the court.
- **Hooks:** a desert crossing by futuristic vehicle; the river-spirit of the Niger.
- **Content note:** YES -- empire-building and enslavement; frame as a clash of river kingdoms, do not glorify the slave-trade element.

**13. Benin, British expedition of 1897** -- Benin, Nigeria
- **Why it works:** a palace city with courtyards and brass/bronze iconography; a dense, sculptural environment.
- **Gender/class:** the oba (king) and warrior guilds (Igban) vs. market women and commoners; the market as a female-dominated space.
- **Hooks:** a futuristic reclamation of the city; the oba's bronze gods animated.
- **Content note:** YES -- colonial violence and the looting of bronzes; frame as a city and its art, handle the colonial context with care.

**14. Ghana independence (1957)** -- West Africa
- **Why it works:** a coastal capital at a historic moment; a positive, forward-looking beat.
- **Gender/class:** workers and women in a newly self-governing state; the pan-African vision.
- **Hooks:** a futuristic pan-African city; a river of gold.
- **Content note:** none.

**15. Timbuktu (13th-16th c.)** -- Mali, West Africa
- **Why it works:** an oasis city with a famous university and mud-brick mosques; a warm, textured environment.
- **Gender/class:** scholars and translators vs. the Dioula merchants; women of the markets.
- **Hooks:** a city of floating libraries; a futuristic archive of the world's knowledge.
- **Content note:** none.

## 4. South Asia

**16. Taj Mahal (1631-1653)** -- India
- **Why it works:** a domed marble mausoleum and garden; a symmetrical, light-rich environment for composition.
- **Gender/class:** imperial patronage vs. the artisan guilds (masons, carvers); a monument built in memory of a woman (Mumtaz Mahal).
- **Hooks:** a futuristic marble city; a pearl of paradise as a mythological object.
- **Content note:** none (Mughal construction labor is a historical note, not a classroom selling point).

**17. Indian Rebellion of 1857** -- India
- **Why it works:** a fortified city (e.g., Jhansi) with a clear defensive story beat.
- **Gender/class:** sepoy common soldiers vs. the East India Company; Rani Lakshmibai, a documented female warrior-queen.
- **Hooks:** a futuristic Jhansi; a goddess of war as a mythological protector.
- **Content note:** YES -- colonial violence and the sieges; frame as a city's defense, keep violence abstract.

**18. Chola naval empire (9th-13th c.)** -- Tamil Nadu, India
- **Why it works:** a harbor city and fleet; strong for water, ship, and trade design.
- **Gender/class:** merchant sailors vs. the court; the maritime class; women of the court and the port.
- **Hooks:** a sky-fleet; a divine king who commands the sea.
- **Content note:** none.

## 5. Middle East

**19. House of Wisdom, Baghdad (8th-13th c.)** -- Middle East
- **Why it works:** a great round library and translation school; an intellectual, warm environment.
- **Gender/class:** scholars and translators (a mixed-class learned body) vs. the court; the merchant-patron of knowledge.
- **Hooks:** a futuristic library-city; the city as a living archive (mythological knowledge).
- **Content note:** none.

**20. Fall of Constantinople (1453)** -- Byzantium / Middle East crossover
- **Why it works:** a great wall and a walled city; a dramatic, iconic environment.
- **Gender/class:** common defenders vs. the Janissaries (an elite corps of converted origin); the women and clergy of the city.
- **Hooks:** a futuristic wall-city; the archangel Michael as a mythological defender.
- **Content note:** YES -- the sack of the city; frame as the wall and the moment, avoid graphic violence.

**21. Persepolis (6th c. BCE)** -- Persia
- **Why it works:** a stepped terrace palace with the "Hundred Nations" relief; a grand, layered environment.
- **Gender/class:** subject peoples (a hundred nations in the tribute relief) vs. the divine king; women of the harem and the court.
- **Hooks:** a futuristic palace of gold; a divine king's court of stars.
- **Content note:** none.

**22. Petra (1st c. BCE)** -- Nabataea, Jordan
- **Why it works:** a city carved into rose-red rock along a canyon; a strong, self-contained environment.
- **Gender/class:** the caravanserai traders (a mixed-class mercantile class) vs. the settled; women of the caravan.
- **Hooks:** a city carved by wind and time; a futuristic hidden oasis.
- **Content note:** none.

## 6. Indigenous Americas

**23. Tenochtitlan (14th-16th c.)** -- Aztec, Mesoamerica
- **Why it works:** a city on a lake with causeways and chinampas; a striking water-and-temple environment.
- **Gender/class:** the calpulli (commoner households) vs. the pipiltin (nobility); women weavers and the merchant class (pochteca).
- **Hooks:** a floating city on a new lake; the Fifth Sun as a mythological engine.
- **Content note:** YES -- the Spanish conquest (disease, violence); frame as the city and its cosmology, not the conquest.

**24. Machu Picchu / Inca (15th c.)** -- Andes
- **Why it works:** a terraced mountain city in the clouds; a strong high-altitude environment.
- **Gender/class:** the mit'a (corvée labor) vs. the curaca (local rulers); the acllas, women weavers of the state.
- **Hooks:** a city in the clouds; the sun god Inti as a mythological presence.
- **Content note:** none (the forced-labor context is a historical note, not a selling point).

**25. Palenque / Tikal (6th-9th c.)** -- Maya, Mesoamerica
- **Why it works:** a jungle city with towering temples; a dense, vertical environment.
- **Gender/class:** the ajaw (king) vs. the commoners; the queen (ajaw) as a documented female ruler.
- **Hooks:** a jungle city reclaimed by the sky; the world-tree (Wakah Chan) as a mythological axis.
- **Content note:** none.

**26. Polynesian voyaging (settlement of the Pacific)** -- Oceania
- **Why it works:** an atoll and a double-hulled voyaging canoe; a clean, open environment for horizon and scale.
- **Gender/class:** the chiefs (ariki) vs. the commoners; the navigator (a specialist class); women of the island.
- **Hooks:** a sky-ocean navigated by star-roads; the demigod Maui as a mythological figure.
- **Content note:** none.

## 7. Europe

**27. French Revolution (1789)** -- France
- **Why it works:** the streets and the Bastille; a dramatic urban environment.
- **Gender/class:** the Third Estate vs. the nobility and clergy; the market women of the March on Versailles.
- **Hooks:** a futuristic Paris; the goddess of liberty as a mythological figure.
- **Content note:** YES -- the Terror and the guillotine; frame as the street and the idea, not the executions.

**28. Florence in the Renaissance (15th c.)** -- Italy
- **Why it works:** the Duomo dome and the Arno; a warm, art-filled environment.
- **Gender/class:** the guilds (wool merchants, weavers) vs. the Medici patronage; women of the workshops.
- **Hooks:** a futuristic Florence; a city of art as a living machine.
- **Content note:** none.

**29. Viking longships (9th c.)** -- Scandinavia
- **Why it works:** a fjord and a carved longship; a strong, clean environment for silhouette.
- **Gender/class:** thralls (enslaved) vs. the jarls (chiefs); the shieldmaiden (a saga figure) and women of the homestead.
- **Hooks:** a sky-longship; the gods (Odin, the Valkyries) as mythological presence.
- **Content note:** YES -- slavery (thralls) and raiding; frame as the ship and the journey, not the raids.

**30. Industrial Revolution / textile mills (18th-19th c.)** -- Britain
- **Why it works:** a factory city of gears and smoke; a dense, mechanical environment.
- **Gender/class:** mill workers (including child labor) vs. the mill owners; women of the mills.
- **Hooks:** a steampunk city; a city of gears as a living machine.
- **Content note:** YES -- child labor and industrial poverty; frame as the machine and the worker, handle the labor history with care.

## 8. Top 5 Strongest Candidates (all-rounders)

Ranked by how well they satisfy every requirement at once: iconic, cross-culture, strong gender/class, fertile for fantasy, and classroom-appropriate.

1. **Battle of Adwa (1896), Ethiopia** -- a documented female military leader (Taitu Betul) plus a documented peasant-origin general (Ras Alula) in one event; a celebrated victory; strong topography; clean content profile. Best gender/class double-angle in the bank.
2. **Great Zimbabwe (11th-15th c.)** -- an iconic, self-contained 3D environment with a built-in gender/class angle (traders, potters) and a natural "city in the sky" hook; no content note; works for P1, P2 (prop: the Great Enclosure gate), and P3.
3. **Imjin War / Hansan Island (1592), Korea** -- a vivid naval environment, a class-mobility story (a commoner rising to admiral), and the "turtle ship" as a ready fantastical prop/character; clean content profile.
4. **Tenochtitlan (14th-16th c.), Aztec** -- the single most visually distinctive Indigenous-American environment (a city on a lake), with a clear commoner-vs-noble class angle and a rich mythological system; strong content note handled by framing as the city and its cosmology.
5. **House of Wisdom, Baghdad (8th-13th c.)** -- a warm, intellectual environment with a strong "city as a living archive" hook and a clean content profile; an easy, positive anchor for a design-thinking course.

**Honorable mentions:** Meiji Restoration (1868, Japan), Petra (1st c. BCE), Samarkand (15th c.), and the 1964 Tokyo Olympics (Japan) are all clean-content, strong-environment candidates with good gender/class angles.

## 9. Week-to-Candidate Mapping (suggestion for the Planner)

This is a **starting sketch**, not a fixed assignment. The principle: match the candidate's strength to the project's deliverable type (P1 = environment, P2 = character/prop, P3 = story moment), and spread cultures so no two adjacent weeks lean on the same tradition.

**P1 - Environment study (W3-W5, Sept 25 - Oct 9).** Pick environment-rich candidates. Suggested shortlist for the P1 prompt list (8-12):
- Great Zimbabwe (11), Tenochtitlan (23), Petra (22), Samarkand (9), House of Wisdom (19), Himeji castle town (4), Machu Picchu (24), Florence (28), Persepolis (21), Timbuktu (15), Viking fjord (29), Polynesian atoll (26).
- These are all strong, self-contained spaces that read well in a single hero render and support 3-5 directional studies (different silhouettes, palettes, scales, flows).

**P2 - Character or prop design package (W6-W8, Oct 16 - Nov 6; midterm crit W7).** Pick candidates with a strong central figure or a distinctive object. Suggested shortlist:
- Characters: a female general (Adwa's Taitu, 10), a warrior-queen (Lakshmibai, 17), an empress-regent (Empress Li, 6), a navigator (26), a shieldmaiden (29), a queen-ajaw (25), a market woman (13, 15, 23).
- Props: the turtle ship (3), a Viking longship (29), a polynesian voyaging canoe (26), a dragon-boat (6), a bronze guardian (13), a pearl-of-paradise object (16).
- Note P2 is character-OR-prop; the bank supplies both tracks. The style-study variant (a required P2 slot) pairs naturally with any candidate that has a named art-style reference (e.g., the oba's bronze look, the Chola harbor look).

**P3 - Previs blockout / story moment (W9-W12, Nov 13 - Dec 4).** Pick candidates with a clear dramatic beat and 2-4 distinct shots. Suggested shortlist:
- Fall of Constantinople (20), Fall of the Ming (5), Battle of Yamen (6), Imjin War / Hansan (3), French Revolution (27), 1964 Tokyo Olympics (7), Ghana independence (14), Meiji Restoration (1), Benin (13), Indian Rebellion of 1857 (17).
- These have a natural beginning-middle-end that maps to 2-4 camera setups, and a deliberate light-mood arc (e.g., dawn-to-dusk for a siege, the stadium lights for the Olympics).

**W1-W2 (foundations/orientation) and W8 (study week / optional posing):** no project prompt needed. W1-W2 use the Starter Scene and Quick Sheet on low-stakes study sprints (any clean candidate above works as a warm-up subject). W8's optional poseable-mannequin side project is the only sanctioned posing slot; it is ungraded and off the critical path, so it does not need a prompt from this bank.

**Content-note handling in the mapping:** when a content-noted candidate (5, 6, 8, 12, 13, 17, 20, 23, 27, 29, 30) is used, the lesson doc should lead with the design question (space, character, or moment) and the fantastical hook, and treat the sensitive historical layer as context the student may or may not draw on. This keeps the event classroom-appropriate while preserving its richness.

## 10. Constraints the Lesson Docs Must Respect

These are carried over from the plan files and must hold for every lesson document the Executor writes.

**Cadence and time.**
- 13 teaching Fridays, Sept 11 - Dec 11, 2026; **one 3-hour session per week; no homework.** Every lesson must be completable in-class within the 3-hour session template (warm-up, one new thing, guided practice, open work, close).
- Out-of-class practice is the default mode but is **stated, not assumed**, and is **2-4 h/week** (named per project). Lesson docs must never require work that cannot be finished in the 3-hour session.
- One learning goal per session; one new tool per tool session; max 1-2 new skills per project.

**Terminology.**
- The sheet deliverable is called a **funpack** (primary term in this program). **"turnaround"** and **"fun sheet"** are accepted aliases. Lesson docs use "funpack" as the primary word and may note the aliases.
- Other terms keep their names: previs blockout, shot sequence (contact sheet), contact sheet, mood board, hero render, blockout, directional study.
- No emoji anywhere. Lowercase-hyphenated filenames. All markdown under 400 lines.

**Tool availability per week (lesson docs should naturally use the relevant tool).**
- **W1:** Starter Scene (P0) is the scaffold for the skill probes and study sprint. Quick Sheet is introduced W1-W2.
- **P1 weeks (W3-W5):** Quick Sheet (contact sheets of 3-5 directional studies), Scale Indicator (blockout gate W4), File/Scene Auditor (grading gate, all projects), Deliverable Packager (P1 due gate W5). Palette Extractor optional for the mood board.
- **P2 weeks (W6-W8):** Funpack/3-View generator (the funpack sheet), Variant & Sequence Composer (variant/style-study sheet), Reference Frame Aligner (style-study reference), Pose Preset Pack only for the optional mannequin side project (W8/show-and-tell). Scale Indicator and Auditor continue to apply.
- **P3 weeks (W9-W12):** Variant & Sequence Composer (sequence mode for the shot-sequence contact sheet), Reference Frame Aligner (thumbnail-to-block matching), Quick Sheet (light-mood comparisons), Auditor and Packager at the due gate (W12).
- Tool-outage fallback: if a tool is unavailable, the teacher provides the manual workflow from the tool's cheat sheet and the requirement stands unchanged. Lesson docs should not hard-depend on a single tool.

**Assessment tilt and deliverables.**
- **60/40 tilt:** 60% design thinking and iteration evidence, 40% technical execution and presentation. Lesson docs should frame every prompt as a design question, not a render target.
- Shared deliverable set per project: one auditor-passing .blend, one presentation sheet, 1-2 hero renders (presentation resolution, not 4K), a 5-minute talk-through.
- **Not required:** animation, rigging, posing (except the optional mannequin side project), topology discipline, game-ready assets, 4K finals.
- P3 is **static by design** (a shot sequence of still frames, not motion).
- Checkpoints are pass/fail gates (week-1 thumbnail/plan, week-2 blockout); a Late-Start Protocol exists (3-day grace, one re-gate, merit grading).

**Scope boundaries (do not cross in lesson docs).**
- Do not write the student-facing lesson documents (Executor's job). Do not re-plan the course (Planner's job). Do not touch plan/, review/, or tools/.
- Prompts are placeholders; the teacher finalizes them. The bank is raw material.
- 2D concepting and paintover are done in the **student's preferred external program** (Photoshop, Procreate, Clip Studio, or their choice); no in-class 2D tooling is mandated.

## 11. Conflicts / Ambiguities for the Planner to Resolve

1. **Content-note policy is not yet defined.** The bank flags 11 candidates with content notes, but the plan does not state how the program wants sensitive events handled in student-facing docs. The Planner should decide the standing rule (lead with the design question + hook, treat the sensitive layer as optional context) and confirm it with the teacher/program.
2. **P2 character-vs-prop track selection.** The bank supplies both tracks, but the Planner must decide whether the P2 prompt list presents a mixed character/prop menu (current plan: student picks one) and which candidates anchor each track.
3. **Culture-distribution across adjacent weeks.** The mapping sketch spreads cultures, but the Planner should confirm no two adjacent project weeks draw on the same regional tradition (e.g., avoid back-to-back Japan + Korea in P1) to keep the bank's cross-cultural intent visible in the actual prompt lists.
4. **Placeholder wording.** Prompts are placeholders now. The Planner should confirm the exact placeholder format ("a place where [event] happens" vs. a named event) and whether the event name appears in the student-facing doc at all.
5. **Funpack primary-term confirmation.** The plan marks funpack as primary with turnaround/fun-sheet as aliases, but flags this for the program advisor. Lesson docs should use funpack as primary until the advisor confirms; if the advisor prefers turnaround, only the label changes.
6. **Tool-dependency language.** Lesson docs should reference tools by name (Quick Sheet, Scale Indicator, Funpack generator, Composer) but include the manual fallback in case a tool is unavailable in a given week. The Planner should confirm the tool names are stable before the Executor writes.
7. **W8 optional mannequin side project.** It is ungraded and off the critical path, but the Planner should confirm whether it appears in the student-facing W8 doc at all (the plan says the teacher does not solicit it) so the lesson doc neither pressures nor omits it inconsistently.

## Sources

- `plan/semester-overview.md` -- course vision, 13-week arc, the three deliverable projects, 60/40 tilt, tooling and freedom guardrails.
- `plan/project-briefs.md` -- per-project deliverables, freedom parameters, checkpoints, rubric sketches, side-project rules.
- `plan/custom-tools.md` -- the ten student-facing tools + foundation module, terminology (funpack primary), build order and ready-by dates.
- `plan/class-structure.md` -- the 3-hour Friday session template, anti-overwhelm rules, cadence assumption.
- `tools/README.md` -- tool set index, build status (10/10 audited), install and per-tool docs.
- `Knowledge_Base/Glossary.md` -- definitions of funpack, turnaround, blockout, directional study, 60/40 tilt, and related terms.
- Wikipedia: "Imjin War" (1592-1598 Japanese invasions of Korea) -- confirms the commoner-militia/class and naval (Hanseon/Hanseong) angles and the turtle-ship subject. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imjin_War
- Wikipedia: "Ras Alula" (Ethiopian general, c.1847-1897) -- confirms the peasant-origin class angle and the Adwa (1896) context; paired with the documented female leader Taitu Betul for the Adwa candidate. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ras_Alula
- Remaining candidates are encyclopedia-grade, widely documented events (Meiji Restoration, Battle of Sekigahara, Fall of the Ming, Battle of Yamen, Great Zimbabwe, Battle of Tondibi, Benin, Timbuktu, Taj Mahal, Indian Rebellion of 1857, House of Wisdom, Fall of Constantinople, Persepolis, Petra, Tenochtitlan, Machu Picchu, Palenque/Tikal, Polynesian voyaging, French Revolution, Renaissance Florence, Viking longships, Industrial Revolution) and are cited by their standard names rather than individual URLs.

title: Detailed Prompt Cards - Part 1 of 3 (Warm-ups + P1 Environments)
body:
This file is the first of three detail cards for the 23 candidates used in the student lesson docs. Part 2 covers the P2 menu (character/prop) first appearances; Part 3 covers the P3 story-moment first appearances, the full-set hook tally, bank corrections, and the shared source list. A candidate used in several weeks appears once, in its first course placement, with a "used in" line listing every placement.

- Part 1 (this file): `research/prompt-details-p1.md` - 1964 Tokyo Olympics, Petra, Great Zimbabwe, Tenochtitlan, Samarkand, House of Wisdom, Himeji, Machu Picchu, Timbuktu, Viking fjord, Polynesian voyaging
- Part 2: `research/prompt-details-p2.md` - Adwa, Jhansi 1857, Battle of Yamen, Palenque/Tikal, turtle ship, Benin 1897, Taj Mahal
- Part 3: `research/prompt-details-p3.md` - Fall of Constantinople, Fall of the Ming, French Revolution, Ghana independence, Meiji Restoration; plus hook tally, corrections, shared sources

How to read each card: the fields are the raw material for the placeholder blocks already in `students/` (W1, W2, W3). The bank's existing hook stays on each card so you can see it next to the new labeled hooks. The design-concept thread is written to stand alone - no event names inside it - for your idea of building standalone design questions on abstract concepts.

---

### 1. 1964 Tokyo Olympics (bank cand. 7)
- **Event:** 1964 Tokyo Olympic Games; postwar Japan, 1964
- **Used in:** W1 warm-up (retro-futurist stadium + torii arch); W9 P3 list (retro-futurist stadium, city in motion)
- **Regional uniqueness:** (1) Japan's modern stadium age opened with this Games - the Yoyogi National Stadium, designed by Kenzo Tange, is the anchor form (web-verified). (2) The torii gate as a symbolic threshold - vermilion, two uprights, crossbeam - is a vocabulary any student will recognize as Japanese. (3) 1964 is the year of the first Shinkansen high-speed rail line, so "old town + new infrastructure" is the documented era texture. (4) Light and color: bright summer daylight, white concrete and vermilion accents.
- **Gender angle:** female athletes and female workers in a rebuilding economy - the bank centers women in the national project of reconstruction, a documented shift in public roles (bank cand. 7).
- **Class angle:** a national project of common effort - workers, athletes, and volunteers rather than an elite court; class is expressed as collective labor and civic spectacle (bank cand. 7).
- **Context note:** none flagged.
- **Hooks:**
  - [futuristic] (bank hook) a retro-futurist Tokyo stadium district, in a city that believes it has always been like this - the W1 warm-up subject.
  - [amalgamation] a stadium district where a Shinkansen train loop and a torii gate are the same structure - the track runs under the arch and the arch is the station canopy.
  - [what-if] the 1964 opening ceremony happens today, in a city that never modernized - old streets, new ceremony, the gates opening for the first time.
  - [mythological] (bank hook) a torii gate arching over the field as a threshold the gods use to watch the races.
- **Design concept thread:** public spectacle versus private routine; a threshold moment (the opening) as the frame that gives meaning to the everyday street.

### 2. Petra, Nabataea (bank cand. 22)
- **Event:** Nabataean caravan city of Petra, 1st c. BCE, modern-day Jordan
- **Used in:** W2 study sprint (city carved by wind and time); W3 P1 list (hidden futuristic oasis)
- **Regional uniqueness:** (1) Architecture is subtractive: facades carved downward into rose-red sandstone cliffs (Al-Khazneh, Ad-Deir), not built up - a distinctive material logic for 3D massing. (2) The landscape is a narrow wadi funneling into open carved spaces - a built-in flow for the eye. (3) Light: morning light rakes the facades from one side only, giving strong directional color (rose, cream, shadow) - the W2 question is built on this. (4) The Nabataeans were renowned water engineers - channels, cisterns, and dams made a desert caravan city possible (web-verified).
- **Gender angle:** women of the caravan and of the household - the bank's angle is the caravan's mercantile women, whose work moved across the same routes as the goods (bank cand. 22).
- **Class angle:** the caravanserai traders - a mixed-class mercantile class - versus the settled community; trade routes made wealth independent of land and birth (bank cand. 22).
- **Context note:** none flagged.
- **Hooks:**
  - [futuristic] (bank hook) a hidden futuristic oasis carved into the canyon walls - blue technology inside rose stone.
